title: I See What You're Thinking
coreMove: Notice the split between polished words and whole-body behavior, then let that split make you more curious rather than more certain.
sourcePressure: The source sidecar frames the opening promise: nonverbal behavior can show comfort, discomfort, interest, hesitation, and direction before speech has fully edited the moment. The chapter must make the whole body matter more than the face alone while refusing mind-reading claims.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version tells readers that body language reveals hidden thoughts. This plan must force the writer to stay with observable comfort, discomfort, interest, hesitation, and direction, then choose a better next question.

hook: A dramatic claim that you can know what someone is thinking before they speak.
A face-only hook built around a fake smile or eye contact.
counterintuition: Most people assume words matter, but actually the body tells the truth.
A single mismatch reveals what someone really means.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and watch someone's body language.
Stare at a stranger until you decode them.
Pick one gesture and decide what it means.

exampleSpecs.domain: hospital discharge instructions after a minor stroke
exampleSpecs.audience: a nurse watching a patient insist he understands the medication schedule
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the patient leaves with unspoken confusion that could send him back to the emergency department
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The nurse hears yes, I have it, but sees the patient smooth the discharge packet twice, keep his eyes on the pill grid, and pull his shoulders inward, so she asks him to walk her through tomorrow morning instead of accusing him of confusion.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stapled discharge packet lies open beside a plastic water pitcher.

exampleSpecs.domain: aquarium touch-tank volunteer briefing a nervous field-trip group
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer who has been trained to keep children moving through the exhibit
exampleSpecs.stakes: one rushed child could yank away, splash the ray, and make the whole group tense
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The volunteer hears the child say she wants a turn, but notices her wet fingers curl under her sleeve, her torso angle behind the acrylic corner, and her eyes track the exit mat, so he offers a dry-shell observation first.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A gray ray glides under a row of dripping child-sized handprints.
mustAvoid: animal-care facts overtaking the body read

exampleSpecs.domain: small-claims mediation over a damaged catering deposit
exampleSpecs.audience: a mediator trying to keep two business owners from hardening too early
exampleSpecs.stakes: a settlement can still happen if the mediator notices the first sign that the public position is not the whole story
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The caterer says the number is final while sliding the calculator away, flattening the invoice with both palms, and glancing at the signed delivery photo, so the mediator asks which part of the bill is hardest to move rather than treating final as final.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A laminated delivery photo sits between two marked-up invoices.

exampleSpecs.domain: independent camera shop helping a customer choose a used lens
exampleSpecs.audience: a clerk who knows the buyer is trying not to look inexperienced
exampleSpecs.stakes: a rushed sale could become a return, while a better question could preserve trust
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The customer says the lens is perfect, but sets the rear cap down crooked, presses the price tag flat, and keeps his body angled toward the beginner shelf, so the clerk decides to ask what he plans to photograph first.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A used 50mm lens rests on a black microfiber cloth.

exampleSpecs.domain: community pottery sale where a buyer says a cracked bowl is fine
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer cashier trying to keep the sale fair without embarrassing the artist
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether politeness hides discomfort that should change the next move
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before asking again, the cashier predicts the buyer's body will answer first; the buyer smiles, but keeps one hand under the crack, lowers the bowl toward the return table, and stops meeting the artist's gaze, so the cashier offers to find the maker's seconds shelf.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A celadon bowl with a hairline crack sits on tissue paper.
mustAvoid: making the smile the whole evidence

exampleSpecs.domain: historic-house tour guide noticing a guest fall silent near a narrow staircase
exampleSpecs.audience: a guide balancing the tour script with visitor comfort
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the guide keeps reciting facts or prevents a visitor from being trapped in a route that feels unsafe
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the stairs, the visitor asks detailed questions and leans toward display cases; at the staircase landing she gives short answers, grips the brochure, and turns her body toward the garden door, so the guide offers the ground-floor route without naming fear.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A polished wooden handrail bends into a tight servant staircase.
mustAvoid: old-house atmosphere replacing the visible body shift

skillTargets: separate a spoken claim from the observable whole-body signals that complicate it
choose a curiosity-based next question when words and body behavior do not line up
identify comfort, discomfort, hesitation, interest, or direction without naming a hidden thought
evaluate whether an interpretation overreaches beyond the visible split

tryThisNowSpec: In your next ordinary conversation, notice one moment when the person's words and body do not point the same way. Write only what you saw and one neutral follow-up question you could ask.
